fields.expected: I built a local Playwright-based job-application agent in TypeScript and Node, where every application moves through an explicit state machine and every mutating capability sits behind fail-closed flags like SUBMIT_ENABLED and FORM_FILL_ENABLED. I built it because job hunting is mostly repetitive browser work, but a fully autonomous browser agent can submit a real application or fabricate an answer with one wrong action, so free-text essays and demographic fields are architecturally prevented from being auto-filled and always generate a human-review item. The hard part was not the automation, it was designing a validation ladder so a capability is only called working once it has been tested against the level of reality it claims to support.

fields.expected: I found the role through an online job board while searching for AI-first engineering internships, and I looked into Xsolla from there. What kept my attention was the framing of the role itself: an AI-first engineering team is one of the few places where the boundary between software engineering, machine learning, and product thinking is not rigid, which is the kind of environment I have been looking for. Most of what I have built sits in that space. I built an iOS health product end to end in Swift and SwiftUI and shipped it into a live Hopkins pilot with 30+ users, and I currently build the machine-learning core of an anomaly-detection system, including the ingestion pipeline, a versioned FastAPI service, and an LLM explanation layer. I care a lot about where automation should stop rather than only where it can go, and a company explicitly building AI into how it engineers seems like a place where that question comes up daily rather than theoretically.
